articles.title_orig: No, China's AI bubble did not burst
articles.title_zh: No, China's AI bubble did not burst
articles.content_orig:
A more nuanced explanation for the recent drop in share price, is that the market is distinguishing between chips that have been purchased and those that actually work
No, China's AI bubble did not burst
The fall was as swift as the rise had been noisy. In less than four months, the STAR 50, which tracks 50 of the largest science and technology innovators listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s STAR Market, lost about 40% of its value. According to a Reuters analysis published on 26 October 2026, roughly $480bn was wiped from the market value of companies listed on the innovation board during the sell-off.
The index is not devoted solely to AI firms. It includes companies working in semiconductors, advanced equipment, biotechnology and other fields. Yet it is heavily exposed to chips and computing, making it a useful, if imperfect, reflection of both the enthusiasm that surrounded China’s technology story and the doubts that have since begun to shadow it.
The decline does not prove that AI is a bubble, nor does it mean that demand for chips and data centres will decline. It does, however, raise questions put aside while share prices were rising: how much are companies spending? How much of their computing capacity are they actually using? And are their expected revenues and profits sufficient to justify what investors have paid?
Even after the correction, the STAR 50’s trailing price-to-earnings ratio remained near 100, after approaching 250 during the rally. That compared with around 30 for the Nasdaq 100. This does not mean that every Chinese company in the sector was overvalued, but it does show how much future growth had already been priced in before it materialised.
AI- and technology-related shares accounted for an estimated 42% of market capitalisation and 57% of trading in mainland Chinese and Hong Kong-listed shares, according to Goldman Sachs figures Reuters cited. When liquidity and expectations concentrate around a single investment track, the market becomes sensitive to doubts about demand, earnings, or companies’ access to advanced technology.
Shares in robotics company Unitree have lost roughly half their value since its August listing, after the offering attracted extraordinary demand. Memory-chip maker CXMT lost more than a quarter of its value in a month, while MetaX and Moore Threads fell to around half their July levels after recording spectacular gains following their stock-market debuts.
A man walks past a brokerage firm in the central business district of Beijing, China, where an electronic display on the glass shows a stock index chart, on 13 October 2025.
No single cause drove the correction. High valuations that were hard to justify with current profits coincided with questions about the durability of demand, tax bills, and the possibility of further US and Western restrictions on the use of Chinese equipment in data centres. Sales by Chinese state-backed investors added to the pressure, as authorities sought to cool speculation and preserve a gradually rising market that would not end in another boom-and-bust.
China’s data centres tell a story that matters more than short-term share-price movements. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology says the occupancy rate for computing-infrastructure racks has reached 71.4%. By contrast, Chinese industry estimates compiled by business publications and research bodies put the actual utilisation of intelligent-computing capacity at around 30-37%, with some public computing centres thought to be even lower.
The two figures are not necessarily contradictory. Rack occupancy means that equipment has been installed in a data centre. Capacity utilisation measures how much time processors spend doing actual work. A centre may therefore be filled with servers while many of them wait for paying workloads or operate far below their potential.
Industry estimates suggest China will have more than 500 intelligent-computing centres by mid-2026. Some, however, were built in response to local-government incentives and investment targets before sufficient commercial demand or adequate network infrastructure existed to distribute workloads efficiently.
At the same time, China continues to face shortages of the most advanced chips, high-speed memory and interconnection components needed to train large models. The situation therefore cannot simply be described as a “computing glut”. It is more accurately a mismatch: less efficient capacity, or capacity in the wrong place, alongside a shortage of the advanced computing resources developers actually need.
A robot interacts with people at the Keenon Robotics booth during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, China, on 18 July 2026.
The question extends far beyond China. The world is building the physical foundations of the AI economy more quickly than the ultimate return on that investment is becoming clear. The International Energy Agency estimates that capital expenditure by the largest cloud-computing providers will exceed $700bn in 2026, with most of the money going into data centres, chips, electricity networks and cooling equipment.
JPMorgan estimates global AI-related capital expenditure at about $900bn in 2026 and says the cumulative total could reach $5.5tn by 2030. Goldman Sachs puts global investment in 2026 at around $1tn. The figures differ because the institutions do not define AI investment in precisely the same way. They nevertheless agree that the world is experiencing one of the largest waves of digital-infrastructure investment in history.
The cost is also visible in the energy bill. Data centres consumed about 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025. The International Energy Agency expects their consumption to approach 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, equivalent to about 3% of global electricity demand.
Direct revenue has not yet caught up with spending. An analysis by the University of California, Los Angeles estimates that the infrastructure built by major investors since 2022 may require annual revenue of $500bn to $650bn to cover depreciation and operating costs and provide an adequate return on capital. By contrast, estimates put the current annual revenue of the leading AI application providers at between $150bn and $218bn.
This comparison is not a final verdict on the viability of the investments. Revenue is growing rapidly, the assets will remain in use for years, and some of the benefits appear as savings within businesses rather than as separate AI revenue. It does, however, illustrate how far the industry still has to travel before its returns match the amount of capital committed to it.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 6 January 2025.
Concerns surrounding AI are no longer confined to whether companies can generate returns commensurate with their spending. Recent developments involving Nvidia, Microsoft and Anthropic show that bottlenecks may also stem from management upheaval, geopolitical restrictions, delays in building data centres and even disruption to the services companies and governments rely on every day.
On 12 November 2026, Nvidia announced that its founder, Jensen Huang, had resigned as president and chief executive and stepped down from the board with immediate effect. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive pending the selection of a permanent successor. The official announcement did not give a reason for Huang’s resignation, but it came days after a governance crisis prompted the board to open an independent investigation. Reports had alleged that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence operation, while separate reports concerning personal relationships raised questions about executive conduct and potential conflicts of interest. articles.title_orig: China says Xi-Trump-Putin summit "conducive to global stability"
articles.title_zh: China says Xi-Trump-Putin summit "conducive to global stability"
articles.content_orig:
China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.
That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.
While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.
"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.
The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.
"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy.
Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success.
China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.
"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.
Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.
U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi and Putin, maybe Kim meeting
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi and Putin, maybe Kim meeting
articles.content_orig:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections
Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.
At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand , push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.
He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.
White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.
The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal , which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.
The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject ; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.
Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.
Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.
Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.
Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine , which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.
However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.
That is believed to be unpalatable to China , which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.
after newsletter promotion
Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.
Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.
Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.
Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.
“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum . “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”
Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.
“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”
With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive chip technology being exported to China .
The interim final rule from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal that led Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week after reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest Asian customers.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
The rule came after growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on its "entity list," which would restrict certain exports to it.
Share prices of Nvidia and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell Monday morning after the interim rule was announced, among them chipmakers Micron Technology , Intel and Advanced Micro Devices .
The rule is designed "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," according to the text of the rule.
The new restrictions "will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using" advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors produced by U.S. companies to train advanced AI models, the rule says.
The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that American authorities began investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed and one of its executives, Alice Huang, in 2024, "after the company started importing billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia."
"Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant," The Times reported that day. "While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China."
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, and that she was a spy working for China. The two are not related. China's government has denied the claim that Alice Huang was a spy.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, as national security advisor, leads the National Security Council, warned President Donald Trump last spring that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, The Times has reported.
Rep. John Mooelnaar, the Michigan Republican who is chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement on the new rule that it "sends a message to the Chinese Communist Party that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years."
"Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy," Moolenaar said. "This new rule is an important step in keeping chips out of ill-intentioned hands, strengthens our national security laws, and will help protect America's lead in the AI race."
Chris McGuire, a former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, in a post on X called the new rule "a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips."
"The work here is not done, as there are some critical loopholes that remain open and need to be closed in a follow-up rule (namely those related to activities inside the United States)," wrote McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. "Commerce should move extremely quickly to close these. But this is the first time in over 18 months that the administration is starting to take export controls seriously, and does represent a meaningful step forward."
McGuire said that the fact that the new rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the NSC "is remarkable and unprecedented."
"I have never seen a BIS rule that was not written by BIS," he wrote. "That implies that Commerce was dragged kicking and screaming over the finish line by the White House and Treasury, and instructed to publish this rule rather than the rumored weaker one that it preferred. Remarkable."
Commerce's new rule was published a day after Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state, the ranking Democrat on the Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, in a letter to Lutnick said that Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance have "used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models."
"These companies are exploiting a loophole in U.S. export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People's Republic of China]," Cantwell wrote.
"Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology," she wrote.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines says it resolved a "widespread system outage," days after nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: United Airlines says it resolved a "widespread system outage," days after nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
United Airlines on Monday said a widespread system outage that delayed flight departures is over.
In a statement early Monday evening, the airline said it had resolved a technology issue linked to the problem, which came on the heels of a nationwide FAA ground stop.
While some flights were delayed, the company said, there was no impact on flights in progress or on United Express flights.
United announced the outage roughly an hour earlier, just before 5 p.m.
The union representing United pilots said in a statement that the outage had affected multiple pilot-facing applications, including crew communications and messaging systems, as well as the airline’s ability to provide final aircraft weight information for departing flights.
The union said it was working with management to better understand the scope of the disruption. Pilots had been advised to follow procedures in the flight operations manual, according to the statement.
A passenger on a United flight bound for Hong Kong told NBC News that a pilot announced that they’d been unable to get performance data for takeoff because of an IT issue. The pilot said they planned on doing “old school” calculations so they could take off, according to the passenger, Halina Eth.
In another announcement, the pilot said that systems were back online and there was a “very narrow window of opportunity to get this flight in the air,” according to a video shared with NBC News.
The issue did not appear to be related to technical issues that prompted the ground stop that halted air travel across the United States for more than four hours Friday evening.
Other airlines did not appear to be affected by Monday’s United issue.
It’s the latest system relied on by millions of Americans to falter . Earlier Monday, JPMorganChase said a technical issue was causing some banking transactions to be delayed for both its own customers and others.
Late Friday, the FAA was forced to issue a nationwide ground stop after a fiber upgrade crashed a critical communication system. By Monday, air travel in the U.S. was largely returning to normal after a chaotic weekend for travelers, crews and airlines.
And last week, Microsoft Outlook went down due to what the tech giant said was a “bug” and overwhelmed servers.
While there is no evidence that any of the issues are related, they seem to be fulfilling concerns about America’s overreliance on aging infrastructure. They’re also occurring against a backdrop of warnings about AI risks and cyberattacks, stoking fears that wider problems may be afoot.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
Tim Stelloh is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Jay Blackman is an NBC News producer covering such areas as transportation, space, medical and consumer issues.

articles.title_orig: Trump Backs Calls for Huang to Be Reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: Trump Backs Calls for Huang to Be Reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Something pretty remarkable is happening in Silicon Valley right now. One shouldn't be surprised, considering the profit motives of many invested in the AI ecosystem and that what Nvidia ( NVDA ) does lies at the center of it all.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as the company's CEO under a cloud of controversy he created, and suddenly some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley are organizing a campaign to bring him back.
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk has signed on to the "Bring Jensen Back" petition. Other prominent executives have joined, including Uber ( UBER ) founder Travis Kalanick — who left Uber unceremoniously after his own string of highly publicized missteps.
Read more: Live updates on Nvidia ahead of the AI chip titan's earnings
The online petition has attracted more than 180,000 signatures. Nvidia employees have also taken to X and LinkedIn to voice their support for Huang.
Let's be clear: Jensen Huang is an extraordinary entrepreneur . A once-in-a-lifetime type of talent. He helped build Nvidia into one of the world's most important companies, with a market cap that neared $5 trillion earlier this year. His impact on the AI revolution is enormous and will not be forgotten.
But here's the issue a lot of people are right to point out: Being a brilliant CEO does not make you untouchable.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to Lori, his wife of more than 40 years. There are serious questions surrounding his relationship with a reported Chinese spy. Additional reports say Jensen had affairs with two Nvidia employees, one of whom, Kimberly Powell , was a direct report.
All of these allegations and the broader circumstances deserve a thorough, independent investigation by the board and the law firm leading it, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. They should not be treated as proven facts.
And that's precisely the point.
This isn't just about one man's personal life. It's about corporate governance, national security, the responsibilities of a CEO, and the standards expected of someone running one of America's most strategically important companies.
Nvidia's board has a responsibility to shareholders, employees, and the country — not to Silicon Valley's celebrity CEO culture.
Jensen Huang absolutely deserves due process. But he is not bigger than Nvidia. And no CEO, no matter how brilliant, should be.

articles.title_orig: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major US banks
articles.title_zh: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major US banks
articles.content_orig:
Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and U.S. Bank are reportedly among the major banks experiencing widespread online outages.
JPMorgan Chase’s systems were coming back online Monday after an hourslong nationwide outage left customers reporting trouble withdrawing funds and accessing their bank accounts.
The disruption was traced to a software release the bank rolled out earlier Monday that affected a subset of its systems, according to an FBI official. There was no indication of malicious or external cyber activity, the official said.
The impact was limited to JPMorgan Chase and transactions at other financial institutions in which JPMorgan Chase was a party, the official said.
The bank also said publicly that the incident was not malicious, and its systems were coming back online.
BANK OF AMERICA TO HIRE 1,000 MORE APPRENTICES, INVEST $150M IN WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT
After logging into the Chase app on November 16, during an online banking outage, one user reported seeing this error message. | Fox News
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," Chase said. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible. This is a technical issue, not cyber-related."
Customers began reporting problems conducting transactions Monday morning. Chase earlier acknowledged an online banking issue in a response to a customer through its Chase Support account on X.
"We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking," Chase Support said. "Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience."
A teller at a Washington, D.C., Chase branch told FOX Business that in-store and online banking issues began around 10 a.m., and had been resolved just after 3 p.m. A branch manager said they had some glitches at the branch but can process most transactions there, on app and online. ATM machines were working as normal, the manager said.
At another branch, a Chase bank employee said the ATMs and banking app were working, but the computer system at the branch had "been up and down."
A JPMorgan Chase bank branch as customers experience disruptions due to a banking technology outage. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a company spokesperson said. "This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us."
Bank of America said its systems were operating normally.
"Bank of America systems have been operating normally today. Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information," the bank said in a statement.
LendingTree analyst Matt Schulz warns customers to watch for scammers exploiting confusion around reported Chase outages. His advice: verify updates directly with your bank and never share personal information with unsolicited callers or messages.
A spokesperson for US Bank also said its users were not experiencing issues.
"U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted," the spokesperson told Fox News. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delay."
BANK OF AMERICA UNVEILS $250B INITIATIVE TO MODERNIZE US INFRASTRUCTURE
PNC Financial Service and Wells Fargo told FOX Business they were not impacted by Monday's events.
Zelle, the digital payment network, said its system was working and operating as normal.
"Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should," the company said in a statement. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
A JPMorgan Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
Zelle’s network operator is a company called Early Warning Services, which is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo, according to The Associated Press.
The outage happened just a week after an historic FAA ground stop of air travel nationwide Friday and a Microsoft Outlook email disruption Thursday.

Last week’s widespread Microsoft 365 outage was driven by three factors, including a software bug undetected since July, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said Monday.
The trend continued Monday evening, with United Airlines reporting a system-wide computer outage.
"We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience," the airlines told one person on X. "We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible. We appreciate your patience while we work through this."
United said the issue was resolved later Monday evening.

articles.title_orig: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.title_zh: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.content_orig:
Data center company Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026. The company is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies. A new Commerce Department rule would restrict that access. Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.content_orig:
California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta's office said the San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT "misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public."
Bonta's office alleged that an AI attack in July — in which OpenAI models broke out of an offline space , connected to the internet and hacked into Hugging Face, a rival AI company — was "entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI's choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight."
OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said in a statement to The Times that the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab."
He said the company has "undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity" since the Hugging Face incident, including by strengthening safeguards across its systems and creating a "framework for additional identification and disclosure" of unintended activity, and will "continue to engage" with Bonta's office "to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."
The company previously called the Hugging Face attack a "warning shot" and pledged to make investments to prevent similar incidents.
Bonta's office said the company's "disregard for the public safety" created a "public nuisance" in violation of a law prohibiting businesses from engaging in "unfair" or "fraudulent" practices.
"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," Bonta said.
The lawsuit directly challenges a rapidly growing industry that has been a massive economic boon to the state . An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined.
The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections.
The lawsuit also follows a public reckoning in recent months over claims from industry insiders that AI technology is developing too rapidly and poses an existential threat to human society.
OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly. Chief Executive Sam Altman and Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki once wrote on their company's website that its "first commitment is to build AI in service of humanity" and in a way that empowers "people broadly," not just a concentrated few.
"We believe the safer future is one where power is broadly distributed, so more of the world can participate in building a resilience ecosystem," they wrote. They went on to say that "AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions."
They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws. "The goal wasn't to stop people from driving — it was to make a powerful technology resilient enough for widespread use," they wrote.
The company called the Hugging Face attack "evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed."
Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta's office said. On Monday, his office said such attacks "may just be the tip of the iceberg," but the scope of the problem isn't fully known because OpenAI hasn't answered "detailed questions" about them.
In its own review of the Hugging Face hack alongside third-party auditors, OpenAI found that more than 700 AI agents began coordinating with each other via thousands of messages to escape containment and begin the unsanctioned attack. Subsequent investigations revealed similar testing of unreleased AI models had resulted in other cyberattacks, including on Wikipedia and government websites — sparking fears that future hacks could undermine increasingly critical infrastructure.
Earlier this year, Trump signed a voluntary safety-standards accord with AI executives to establish AI protocols. California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors .
Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release.
"This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated," OpenAI said in a statement.
Bonta said Monday that securing public safety will require litigation and legislation in all 50 states and at the federal and international levels — and that he refused to accept that society should "pass off the blame to machines" while letting those who create them escape accountability.
"The people who created, who create, and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions," Bonta said at a news conference Monday.
"Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: Don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards," he said.
Bonta's office said it is encouraging "anyone with information relevant to this case" to contact it at oag.ca.gov/report .
He said his office is also watching other AI companies "closely," but declined to elaborate.

articles.title_orig: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.title_zh: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-four Shia Muslims, most of them clerics, have been sentenced to life in prison in Bahrain on Iran-linked terrorism charges, according to a UK-based human rights group.
The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) said another five people were handed 15-year prison sentences by the High Criminal Court in Manama.
The advocate general confirmed the sentences but did not give the number of defendants or identify them. He said they were accused of establishing a terrorist group linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
BIRD condemned the verdicts, saying there had been "credible allegations of torture, coerced confessions, and severe restrictions on the defence".
Authorities in the Sunni Muslim-ruled kingdom have reportedly detained hundreds of people, most of them members of its Shia majority, on suspicion of espionage and terrorism offences since the start of the US and Israel's war with regional Shia power Iran in February.
Dozens have also been stripped of their Bahraini citizenship after being accused by the government of "sympathy and praise for Iran's hostile and criminal acts".
Iran has launched thousands of missiles and drones at Bahrain and other Gulf Arab states hosting US forces during the war. On Sunday, the Bahraini military said it had intercepted "several Iranian aerial attacks".
Fifty-six of the defendants sentenced on Monday were arrested in May and June.
BIRD said 47 of them were Shia clerics - including Sheikh Mohammed Sanqour and Sheikh Ali al-Sadadi, who led Friday prayers at the Imam al-Sadiq Grand Mosque in Duraz, and Sayed Moosa al-Alwedaie, who served as imam at the Grand Mosque in Ras Rumman - and nine were their affiliates, including religious reciters.
The 13 other defendants - including the exiled cleric Sheikh Isa Qassim, who holds the religious rank of ayatollah and ​is widely regarded as the spiritual ​leader of Bahrain's Shia community - were tried in absentia, it said. Bahraini authorities said most of them were in Iran.
The 64 defendants faced charges including establishing a terrorist group, which the Public Prosecution said was linked to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), and calling for the suspension of the provisions of the constitution and a change in the system of government.
The prosecution alleged that they had incited terrorist acts and promoted "Velayat-e Faqih" (rule by the supreme jurist), which is the backbone of Iran's theocratic system.
The High Criminal Court convicted all the defendants and imposed prison sentences ranging from 15 years to life, the advocate general and head of the Terrorist Crimes Prosecution announced . The court also fined some of the defendants $265,000 (£200,000) and ordered the confiscation of $21.2m (£16m) for charitable purposes.
The director of BIRD, Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, said the verdicts were "deeply unjust" and constituted "an attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain's Shia community".
Reuters news agency cited a person close to the clerics' defence teams as describing the sentences as "worse than anything we imagined".
Last week, BIRD, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International were among 20 human rights groups which signed an open letter calling on Bahraini authorities to investigate what they described as "serious allegations of torture" in the case.
They said defendants had reported being "subjected to forced standing, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, sleep deprivation, and threats of physical and sexual violence against themselves and their families, as well as citizenship revocation and deportation". Many were pressured to sign lengthy statements they were not allowed to read, they added.
A spokesperson for the Bahraini government said the defendants "were not prosecuted for their beliefs, but were convicted of criminal acts" based on evidence that included seized documents, devices and recorded sermons.
They also said that the Public Prosecution was "careful to ensure the lawfulness of every step and the legality of all evidence obtained".
"Throughout the investigation, all defendants in custody were afforded their full legal rights and safeguards, were able to contact their families, and received healthcare in detention in accordance with the law," they added.

articles.title_orig: After claiming election stolen, Netanyahu allies face their own meddling allegations
articles.title_zh: After claiming election stolen, Netanyahu allies face their own meddling allegations
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing calls from lawmakers for an investigation following a report that alleged that a member of his staff provided information to police against Arab citizens in an attempt to influence last month’s elections. The claims, which Netanyahu’s office denies, were made on an Israeli TV news show this weekend.
The controversy centers on the widely publicized arrest of three activists from the Arab party Raam in southern Israel early on the morning of the October 27 election over an alleged cash-for-votes scheme. Throughout the day, Netanyahu and his Likud party repeatedly amplified the arrests to mobilize their own voters, alleging Raam was trying to “steal the elections.”
Courts later rejected police requests to keep the suspects in custody, saying that the arrests were carried out without a valid search or arrest warrant. All suspects have since then been released.
According to an investigation by Channel 12’s “Uvda,” the allegation originated in Netanyahu’s office. The day before the elections, the report alleges, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, bypassed standard reporting channels and personally contacted the police commissioner to alert him about the activists, passing on information.
Norden allegedly referred police to a separate source who was said to hold information about the activists. But the source was a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office, the report said.
Based on Norden’s complaint and the information provided by the former employee, police carried out the arrests on election day, the report alleged.
On Monday evening, Israel’s Attorney General said she would hold a discussion on the transfer of information from the Prime Minister’s Office to the police. “As part of the discussion, all aspects relating to the matter will be examined,” the Attorney General’s spokesperson said in a statement.
Netanyahu’s office strongly denied the Channel 12 report, saying it was “false and grounds for libel,” but confirmed that Nordan had passed information to the police.
“Criminal information reached Chief of Staff Ido Norden, he fulfilled his duty as expected of any law-abiding citizen and connected that person to the police,” his office said in a statement Sunday evening. Norden learned on the morning of the elections that a person “was indeed caught with tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Raam slips,” the statement continued, referring to a suspect who had already been released.
In a statement, Israel Police said it would examine “the decision-making processes, the chain of reporting, the working interfaces between the relevant police units, and the division of responsibility” related to the allegations in the Channel 12 report. “All police actions, including the operation carried out on election morning, were taken out of commitment and transparency toward the public, and with the aim of protecting the integrity of the elections,” police said.
On Monday evening, the Attorney General requested a pause in this examination until there is a decision “on the appropriate format for the inquiry.”
The main opposition party is calling for an immediate investigation. Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar and a candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said the conduct of Netanyahu and his circle is “a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” warning that “as long as Netanyahu is in office, there will be no more fair and proper elections in Israel.”
Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
Two Arab parties that saw record voter turnout in the elections also demanded an immediate criminal investigation.
“The arrest of our activists in the Negev on the morning of the elections and the attempt to silence Arab Knesset members, if proven, is a direct attack on the integrity of the elections and the will of the voters,” Raam said in a statement, referring to Israel’s parliament. The Joint List called to establish an independent commission of inquiry – the state’s highest investigative body – and suspend all involved police and Shin Bet officials.
“Netanyahu tried to steal our vote, but our vote is what will bring him down. His place is not in the Prime Minister’s Office, but in the interrogation room and before the court,” the party said in a statement.
Since losing his parliamentary majority in the October 27 vote, Netanyahu and his allies have raised various allegations against the Arab parties, accusing them of bribery, foreign funding, and fraud. David Zini, the director of the Shin Bet domestic security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, has pressed to investigate Arab politicians over allegations of foreign interference, but so far hasn’t presented any public evidence to support the allegations against them. According to the Channel 12 report, Zini demanded to wiretap five Arab lawmakers before election day.
The request was refused at the last minute by the attorney general because he did not present any evidence to back his request, Channel 12 reported.
In a statement, the Shin Bet said it carried out “various activities in accordance with its powers under the law.”
Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the Yisrael Beitenu party and the interim chair of the crucial Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said on Monday that he would summon the Shin Bet and police chiefs to discuss alleged foreign interference attempts in the election.

articles.title_orig: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.title_zh: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Andy Burnham laid out his case for reigniting the decade-old Brexit debate at an opulent London banquet Monday, claiming Britain lost more than it gained by leaving the EU.
Delivering his first major foreign policy speech at the Lord Mayor’s banquet in London, Burnham said he will sit down with EU leaders following Friday’s U.K.- EU reset summit — where the two sides are expected to sign an agri-food trade deal, link their emissions trading systems, and establish a new system of visas for young people— to work out “options for our long-term relationship.”
“This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next parliament. At every stage, the British people will be the boss”, Burnham said.
The U.K. prime minister set out his ambition to build a closer U.K. relationship with the EU at his first Labour conference as leader in September — confirming weeks later his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime.
But he is treading a fine line with some members of his own Cabinet, who hold differing views on how far the U.K. should realign with the bloc and whether red lines — including rejoining single market or the customs union — should be crossed.
“This is not about re-running the arguments of 2016,” the U.K. prime minister said, while stressing any new arrangement in this parliament will not breach Labour’s 2024 manifesto, must improve the existing Brexit deal, and benefit working people struggling with the cost of living.
Lamenting Brexit as “exactly what our enemies wanted,” the British prime minister said the U.K.’s withdrawal from the EU had been the “first domino to fall in a global move towards isolationism and protectionism.”
“In the decade since Brexit, our standing in the world has diminished,” he said. “We treated both allies and institutions with insufficient care, and the effects went beyond Europe.”
Burnham joked during the speech that it was a stretch talking about the “Makerfield test” — a reference to the views of his Brexit-voting constituents in Greater Manchester — while wearing white tie and having just received a trumpet salute.
Ahead of Monday’s speech, former Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson — who signed Britain’s post-Brexit settlement with Brussels in 2020 — warned Burnham against “wasting his premiership” relitigating the European question.
“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win — because the reality is that people are not fools,” Johnson said in an interview with the Telegraph newspaper published Monday .
Burnham acknowledged it would “be easier to say nothing about the EU,” but said the hard Brexit deal Britain struck  with the bloc ended with “Britain eventually leaving on bad terms, with bad feeling.”
“To be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years,” he said, “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage — a key figure in the 2016 Brexit campaign — accused Burnham of a “total betrayal” in October when the prime minister prompted speculation he would open the door to restoring freedom of movement.
Polling conducted by Ipsos in October found that 56% of Britons would vote to apply to join the EU and 51% said they would support a referendum after the next general election.

articles.title_orig: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.title_zh: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.
Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.
Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership.
The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy.
The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy.
But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

articles.title_orig: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.title_zh: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase says bank transactions are back to normal after outage online and at some branches
Chase Bank said transactions were posting normally Monday evening after a nationwide outage that had some customers reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.
“Transactions are now posting normally,” a Chase spokesperson said around 6:30 p.m.
The outage began Monday morning, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
Chase said at around 4 p.m. on X that “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware system” and that it was working to resolve it.
The issues had been affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
The issue was not “cyber-related,” the bank said, and did not  impact the entire banking system. “Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”
The bank said that customers still had access to their accounts and funds, but some transactions were taking longer than normal.
Regulators were in touch with the big banks affected “immediately,” a person familiar with the situation said earlier Monday. They “quickly determined this was contained and service was already in process of restoration,” the person said then.
The issues at Chase were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.
It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.
By late afternoon Monday, several Chase bank branches in Manhattan appeared to be operating normally. Customers leaving a branch at 6th Avenue and W. 51st Street told NBC News they didn’t know there had been a problem until they arrived at the branch, where they were told by employees that they’d gotten there at just the right time.
“This is really retail banking,” and not tied to the rest of JPMorgan Chase, said a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The issues with Chase accounts also appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
A spokesperson for PNC Bank said it was “not experiencing any direct impact. We are aware of reports of transaction delays outside of the bank, but those appear to be resolving.”
Truist bank said its services “are operating normally,We continue to closely monitor our systems and are not aware of any broad service disruptions at this time.”
Customers at Wells Fargo also experienced delays, but the company did not provide a statement.
Citibank likewise declined to comment.
A spokesperson for Capital One said the bank “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time.”
— WMAQ’s Lauren Stauffer and Leigh Lesniak contributed reporting from Chicago.

articles.title_orig: Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
articles.title_zh: Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
articles.content_orig:
GUATEMALA CITY (AP) — Guatemala's interior and defense ministers on Monday inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras, days after President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency to curb drug-related violence in the Central American country.
The decree, announced on Saturday, suspends for 30 days several constitutional rights, including freedom of movement and assembly, and allows security forces to disperse groups by force, make arrests and enter homes without warrants.
Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said Monday that the emergency measure also targets groups allegedly linked to drug trafficking that are involved in illegal jade and gold mining in the region.
"We are carrying out a series of coordinated and planned actions with the Defense Ministry and the public prosecutor's office. We have a plan that we will execute over 30 days," Villeda said.
Defense Minister Henry Sáenz said authorities are "establishing territorial control through checkpoints on routes and patrols along roads bordering Honduras."
This area in the eastern part of Guatemala has been the scene of a wave of violence over the past three months.
On Sept. 27, an armed attack left eight people dead in the municipality of Huité, in the department of Zacapa.
Initially, the army claimed the attack involved clashes between organized crime groups; however, days later, it announced that 107 military personnel had been placed at the disposal of the authorities to determine their potential involvement in the massacre, which claimed the lives of three women, including a young girl.
The prosecutor's office is investigating whether the army's actions were linked to the detention of suspected drug traffickers.
Separately, on Nov. 7, Congressman Julio César Portillo Paz and three members of the National Civil Police — who were part of his security detail — were gunned down by armed men in broad daylight in the municipality of Río Hondo, also in Zacapa.
Early on Friday morning, five people were killed in the same department. According to preliminary investigations, armed men arrived in several vehicles at a small village and abducted a man, whose whereabouts remain unknown. They then killed his mother, two brothers and two friends at the scene.
Also on Friday, the U.S. State Department designated three local drug-trafficking groups as terrorist organizations for financing violence and crime in the region. Among those designated are two family clans — Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza — which, according to authorities, maintain deep ties to Mexican drug cartels and operate within the area.

articles.title_orig: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.title_zh: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
articles.title_zh: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
articles.content_orig:
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it .
In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.
The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.
"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.
She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.
She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.
Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.
She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."
The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.
"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.
"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."
The committee hearings continue.
