articles.title_orig: Women stranded by FAA ground stop buy a Bronco for a 27-hour road trip home
articles.title_zh: Women stranded by FAA ground stop buy a Bronco for a 27-hour road trip home
articles.content_orig:
Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota.
She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco.
Travelers across the U.S. were left scrambling Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration announced that it was grounding all flights as it saw inconsistencies in radar data and communications. Officials said that 20,000 flights were affected in the hourslong ground stop, with 12,000 “unable to recover” after the order lifted. Thousands more flights were either delayed or canceled the next day as airlines scrambled to recover service.
Harding, a nurse practitioner who owns a clinic, was ready to get home Friday after being in town for a training with two of her employees. Her group had been at the airport for about 30 minutes when the ground stop occurred.
All three women started out trying to find options through Delta Air Lines, but flights were delayed and rebooked until they gave up the idea of getting in the air altogether, Harding said.
“In the midst of all of that, though, we’re like, ‘We should probably look at trying to get a rental car,’” Harding said. “So we were trying to look, all three of us at one time, trying to get a rental car. There was zero available rental cars within a four-hour radius.”
Uber? No rides to Bismarck.
Overwhelmed and out of ideas, Harding called her husband to ask what she should do. He relayed to her an idea from his mom.
“She said, ‘Why don’t you guys go buy a car?’” Harding recalled.
At that point, the women had been trying unsuccessfully to rebook their flights or find alternatives for more than an hour.
So they started texting with a sales agent at a Ford dealership who promised to stay open while they waited 30 minutes for an Uber out of the Charlotte Douglas International Airport. They arrived at 7:45 p.m. and left with a new Bronco less than two hours later.
Harding said the process gave her an adrenaline rush.
“When we were leaving the airport, I was three-way calling with my husband, the car dealer and my employees, and we were looking at each other like, ‘Is this really happening right now?’” she said.
Harding said she knows it sounds “insane,” but she did what she had to do, relying on a problem-solving instinct she tied to being both an entrepreneur and a nurse.
“If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she said. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.”
Even picking a Ford Bronco was a rushed decision, she said. Harding and her husband were discussing getting a vehicle with a good resale value, but her husband suggested getting a “fun” car just in case they couldn’t sell it once she got home.
“And being a Ford girl, I was like, ‘Broncos look kind of cute and fun,’” she said.
Driving the Bronco off the lot, the women drove 27 hours nonstop to Bismarck, making the most of the trip together. They had a rotation on who would sleep and who would drive.
“We took turns napping, stopped at gas stations and drive-thrus for food,” she said.
Despite the hefty price tag, Harding said she has no regrets about her decision. The women bonded over the journey, and in the end, they have a great story to tell, she added.
As for the Bronco, Harding said it’ll be with her for the long haul.
“I slept 12 hours when I got home, and when I woke up, my husband had drove it three times, and he said he wants to keep it,” Harding said. “So, we’re keeping it.”
Tom Costello is an NBC News correspondent based in Washington, D.C.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock valuation looks 'draconian,' even without Jensen Huang: Analyst
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock valuation looks 'draconian,' even without Jensen Huang: Analyst
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock slid 4.12% Monday in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation , leading a broader chipmaker selloff after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week.
The continued decline since Huang's resignation brought Nvidia's stock to its lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk , rallied behind him. A source familiar with the matter told CNBC, however, that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Huang.
Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal.
Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom.
Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive.
He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.
A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.
In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted at night on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, and more than 150 more throughout Monday.
The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion
Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.
Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access
articles.title_zh: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia .
The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang , became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.
Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.
By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.
Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.
Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18 , the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported .
Trump on Monday denied being briefed . Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz . Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.
A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.
Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war .
"Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses .
Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.
Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."
It wasn't always that way.
At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.
That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters .
Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock .
For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge , according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.
The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales . A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.
Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund , would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported .
But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported .
Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips . His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.
In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.
Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job , the Times reported.
With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.
Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

articles.title_orig: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.title_zh: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.content_orig:
What happens next in Yemen may send fresh shockwaves to the world economy
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.
Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.
Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.
The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.
Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.
But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.
Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?
When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.
The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.
But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.
On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.
Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."
He warns that if the port of Aden â a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants â was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".
But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.
"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."
"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."
It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.
The former British defence attachÃ© to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.
He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.
"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.
"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

articles.content_orig:
Adam Feuerstein, a senior writer and biotech columnist, is the author of Adam’s Biotech Scorecard , a subscriber-only newsletter about the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology.
Adam Feuerstein is a senior writer and biotech columnist, reporting on the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology. He is also a co-host of the weekly biotech podcast The Readout Loud and author of the newsletter Adam’s Biotech Scorecard. You can reach Adam on Signal at stataf.54.
A cancer immunotherapy from CG Oncology delivered into the bladders of patients reduced the risk of tumor recurrence by 68% compared to current medical practice — positive study results announced Monday that may change the way physicians treat certain patients with bladder cancer.
The CG Oncology treatment, called cretostimogene, is made from a type of common cold virus engineered to target cells that express a specific mutation found in bladder tumors. Physicians use a catheter to infuse “creto” directly into the bladder, where it enters the mutated cancer cells, replicates rapidly, then breaks open the cells, killing them.
The randomized Phase 3 study enrolled 367 patients with intermediate-risk bladder cancer, a localized form of the disease that is typically removed in a minimally invasive surgical procedure. Patients are then monitored every three months. If the cancer returns, repeat surgical procedures can be performed, but over time, patients lose bladder function and the cancer can continue to grow.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon
articles.title_zh: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon
articles.content_orig:
Fearing for the safety of American troops, the U.S. Army will build concrete bunkers across the Middle East.
The Army wants 17 bunkers capable of remaining intact through indirect fire attacks, such as from missiles and drones. Ten bunkers are planned for Israel, five in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon, according to an Army notice posted Friday.
The bunkers are meant to replace current personnel shelters made of converted shipping containers, the notice says.
“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace nonstandard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized, precast, reinforced concrete Indirect Fire bunkers,” states the Army’s Sources Sought notice . The deadline for companies to respond to the notice is Nov. 25.
“The objective is to safeguard U.S. and coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility,” the notice continues.
The project comes after Iranian missiles and drones devastated multiple American bases in the Persian Gulf and killed at least 23 personnel . This includes a March 2026 strike on an Army command post in Kuwait that killed six service members. Subsequent reports allege that the site was poorly protected against aerial bombardment.
The Army did not specify the exact locations of the new bunkers.
“Specific base installation names and coordinates” will be released only to eligible contractors once the actual solicitation is released,” the Army said.
Still, the notice refers to the bunkers being emplaced at five “primary installation” sites: one in Israel and two each in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon.
The bunkers appear to be standardized designs meant for quick construction, rather than elaborate fortifications. Each bunker will consist of three sections of reinforced concrete with steel entrance doors and concrete Alaska barriers shielding the entrances. Sandbags will provide additional protection to the exterior walls, and more layers of sandbags will add at least 18 inches of cover to the roof.
The Army intends to move fast. The notice emphasizes that the project must be completed within 45 days after the task order.
“Due to extreme operational urgency (soldiers currently at risk using non-standard containerized shelters), the subsequent solicitation is anticipated to have an expedited 3-day quote turnaround window,” the notice states.
To make this happen, the Army is looking for “qualified, capable, and licensed construction and engineering firms with immediate cross-border and local mobilization capabilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the State of Israel, and the Republic of Lebanon.”
Contractors must specify whether they are bidding to operate in all three nations or only specific countries.
Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

articles.title_zh: Megaspeed says Alice Huang, alleged spy in Nvidia affair scandal, left in 2025
articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump reported trades this year that suggest he has held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock, disclosures that will likely escalate scrutiny into the president’s relationship to the AI giant and his administration’s oversight of an industry at the center of international scandal.
Financial disclosures, reviewed by The Washington Post, revealed that the president’s Nvidia stakes grew sharply from an estimated $615,000 to $1.3 million at the end of 2024 to as much as $62 million within the last year. The latest filings ​do not capture trades from the past two months, meaning that the values could be even higher.
The disclosures follow Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO after the revelation of his extramarital affair with ‌Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , who is accused of having intelligence ties to Beijing.
White House officials have repeatedly maintained that the president does not personally pick or trade individual stocks and Trump has rejected calls to divest his stock holdings. Trump’s assets are in a trust managed by his children and independent financial managers handle his portfolio, according to the White House.
But enormous growth of the president’s financial stakes in Nvidia are in parallel to the president’s close relationship to Jensen Huang and the administration’s regulatory moves that have opened the door for the company to do business in China. The president has routinely defended his administration against criticism over export controls that appear to have been lucrative for both Nvidia and the president.
Nvidia’s stock is trading at roughly $157.72, down over 3.1 percent on the day, as investors react to Huang’s blockbuster resignation ahead of a third-quarter earnings call scheduled for Tuesday.
The company’s board, however, is not considering bringing him back, according to CNBC.
Huang’s resignation last week followed news of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. officials have suspected Alice Huang of spying for China, and the Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed breached U.S. export restrictions.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined Alice Huang had been recruited to influence Jensen Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.
Trump, however, appeared to cast doubt on his own administration’s assessment.
“I don’t know that she’s a spy at all. Nobody's proven that,” he told reporters outside the White House on Monday.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy,” he said.
“Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” he continued, “I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t.”
According to The New York Times , State Secretary Marco Rubio drafted a classified memorandum on Alice Huang’s alleged scheme and had even briefed the president about her suspected activities while the pair were traveling to China on Air Force One in May — months before Jensen Huang’s admission of the affair.
But Trump reportedly brushed the warnings aside and maintained his relationship with the tech mogul, who frequently appeared at the White House and donated $25 million to the president's ballroom project.
Asked on Monday whether he trusted the intelligence that Rubio reportedly provided him, Trump appeared to suggest he thought the reporting was false.
“Who told me that?” he told reporters. “I haven’t heard that.”
Congressional watchdogs are eager to dive into the president’s stocks and his administration’s policies surrounding AI and Nvidia, which include easing Biden-era export restrictions on American AI chips to China in May 2025. That decision opened the door for Nvidia to sell its chips to approved Chinese customers later that year, with a portion of revenue to the U.S. government.
In December, Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 chips to approved customers in China, with 25 percent of the revenue going to the U.S.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this summer whether the government should investigate Trump’s purchase of as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock — just one week before the Commerce Department formalized those export restrictions. Bessent responded by suggesting that Congress should look into banning its own members from stock trading before looking to the White House.
Trump has sought to diffuse tension among his Cabinet officials in wake of the scandal, following reports that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick prevented U.S. oversight on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China.
That reportedly escalated to a Situation Room showdown between Lutnick and Bessent, who appeared to put the blame on the Commerce chief during an appearance on CNBC last week.
The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all “were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent told the network.
Notably not on that list: Commerce Department.
Trump, however, appeared to acknowledge that Lutnick likely resisted putting Megaspeed — seen as a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls — on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.
“He was doing that because you could have — if you didn’t delay it, If you didn’t do something — you could have a blow up with China,” Trump said Monday. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I’ll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides.”
Republican and Democratic members of Congress, meanwhile, are jockeying for Jensen Huang to testify before several committees.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft reveals hidden bug behind global Outlook and Microsoft 365 outage
articles.title_zh: Microsoft reveals hidden bug behind global Outlook and Microsoft 365 outage
articles.content_orig:
A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”
Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.
The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates .
Microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.
The second factor was server load. Microsoft said that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The company keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused new connection requests.
The traffic shift exposed a third factor: infrastructure capacity. An existing fault meant that Microsoft’s gateway server fleet was operating at 14 percent below optimal conditions. That missing headroom could have normally absorbed the demand, but when combined with the changed traffic patterns and underlying defect, it left the gateways with lock contention as requests kept piling up.
As US business operations began hitting their daily peaks, the gateway servers began to freeze. Backup systems that shifted requests away from unresponsive servers did their job, but were met with the same lockouts on the supposedly healthy backup gateways. This created a snowball effect, leaving more than 80 percent of Microsoft’s affected gateway servers frozen in the sweep. Mechanisms in place to isolate affected systems by region seem to have failed. Microsoft’s current report doesn’t address why these isolation systems may have failed.
Recovery took longer than normal because the fix required a targeted system update from Microsoft engineers. Attempts to restart the gateway servers were ineffective; when the servers came back online, large request queues were still waiting for access, immediately triggering the same resource exhaustion that contributed to the outage in the first place. Microsoft says that services like Teams, OneDrive, and other Office applications could be routed away from the affected infrastructure, but scaling limitations stopped Exchange Online from making a similar move.
Since the bug from July was still undiscovered, system rollbacks were equally ineffective. Simply returning to a previous state where things were “working” couldn’t happen, because the ghost was already in the machine. Servers were patched and returned to service gradually, and Microsoft says it has added additional capacity and traffic-distribution guardrails to try to avoid anything similar happening again. Microsoft also extended delivery timeouts on affected emails to stop delayed messages from bouncing back as undeliverable.
Microsoft expects to publish its full final incident report on November 20. This final report may provide additional clarification on why the regional isolation systems failed and what corrective actions will be taken to ensure this type of outage can be avoided in the future. All of Microsoft’s cloud services appeared online and operational as of Monday morning.

articles.title_orig: Russia says its defenses intercepted over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in a major attack
articles.title_zh: Russia says its defenses intercepted over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in a major attack
articles.content_orig:
The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate  has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title_orig: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
articles.title_zh: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
articles.content_orig:
An aerial shows a 49.5 megawatt three-level data center under construction on Oct. 29, 2026 in Vernon, California.
America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability .
The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models , has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers .
American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.
“Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper.
The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions.
They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh.
More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark.
Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption.
However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.
“For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.”
Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF.
The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025.
The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably.
“We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

articles.title_orig: OpenAI sued by California over 80 ‘loss of control’ incidents
articles.title_zh: OpenAI sued by California over 80 ‘loss of control’ incidents
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday Nov. 16, 2026. In the complaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. California Department of Justice/Screenshot by NPR hide caption
California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.
"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."
In the complaint , California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."
That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than what outside researchers have independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.
In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."
After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents – the attack on Hugging Face over the summer – the company admitted that it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI started disclosing voluntarily to the public.
Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have. Major AI companies have since signed onto an agreement organized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.
Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

articles.title_orig: Xbox Is Releasing Two First-Party Expansions In December 2026
articles.title_zh: Xbox Is Releasing Two First-Party Expansions In December 2026
articles.content_orig:
December is often a very quiet month for new game releases, and that's particularly going to be the case in 2026 due to GTA 6 's arrival and the desire from publishers to get as far away from it as possible, but we've still got the likes of Rayman Legends Retold and Stage Tour to look forward to, along with a couple of first-party Xbox expansions.
In terms of first-party stuff, Xbox is initially releasing a paid DLC pack for Minecraft Dungeons 2 on December 1st called The Humblers Awaken. This DLC is included with the Deluxe Edition of the game if you bought it, and it'll be available separately as well.
You can expect "new quests, unexplored environments, colorful cosmetics, and an expanded arsenal of powerful gear" in The Humblers Awaken, while base game players will also be treated to a free update on the same day, adding in new challenges, weapons and armour.
Then, just a day later, Xbox and Obsidian are releasing a first expansion for The Outer Worlds 2 , known as Side Effects Guaranteed. This DLC includes a new narrative story (that'll be concluded in the second part next year), a new region of Elysium Valley to explore, new threats, new perks and an increased level cap.
There's also new weapons, armours, outfits, flaws, a new radio station - you get the picture!
Side Effects Guaranteed will cost $14.99 USD when it arrives on December 2nd, or you'll get it included if you bought either the Premium Edition or Premium Upgrade Edition of The Outer Worlds 2.
Perhaps there's a chance we might get even more from Xbox's first-party studios in December, but as mentioned, it's typically a month where the releases die down. In any case, it's nice to see two expansions on the way very soon!
The Sift is in danger! Something ancient is stirring beneath the ground of the new dimension – a threat that has slumbered for ages and is now beginning to wake. Gather your trusty allies, venture deep into unexplored reaches, take on the not-so-happy humblers, and confront the foes behind their rude awakening!
Side Effects Guaranteed is the first chapter of a two-part expansion for The Outer Worlds 2. A distress signal beckons you and your crew of the Incognito to a derelict ship, where you discover the ship’s crew in suspended animation to keep themselves alive, as they’ve been infected with something that causes explosive cell death. The hunt for a cure leads to Elysium Valley, a brand-new region on Eden.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.title_zh: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.content_orig:
More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue last fiscal year was generated by China – a massive cut that shows the size of the chip giant’s murky business with the US adversary, according to a report.
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang helped power an ecosystem in which it sold its most powerful chips to east Asian data centers that in turn powered tech offered by Chinese tech giants like Alibaba, according to reports.
Such deals drove more than a fifth of Nvidia’s revenue during the previous fiscal year, according to Culper Research, the short-selling firm that originally called out Nvidia’s China issues in May.
Huang’s efforts to supply China with key AI tech showered Nvidia with an eye-watering $12.4 billion in revenue in the six months through July 26 of this year, or 7% of its global revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal, which added that countless more billions of dollars could ultimately trace back to Chinese customers.
The dealings were a workaround to US export controls that sought to keep Nvidia’s top-of-the-line tech out of the hands of Chinese firms – and proved to be a cash cow for the chip giant, according to the Journal report .
As the full extent of Nvidia’s lucrative China business emerges, the Commerce Department announced Monday it is nixing the provision that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
Despite US export restrictions that have thwarted US chip sales directly to China, Nvidia sold chips to firms that set up data centers in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia which then sold the computing power to Chinese tech giants.
Some of those firms – including Singapore-based Megaspeed , which was led by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy and mistress to the former Nvidia CEO – have even been suspected of forwarding chips directly to China.
Between March 2024 and June 2025, Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips to companies in China, according to the WSJ report.
Shipment records show orders for several hundred thousand of the type of chips that US regulations intended to keep out of Chinese hands. The report notes that records don’t specify how many of the chips were actually delivered or where they originated from.
The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third-party countries, according to a Monday press release .
A license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion,” according to the new rule .
In a Sunday letter addressed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington – the top Dem on the Senate Commerce Committee – urged the Commerce secretary to reinforce export controls on the sale of AI chips to China.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote. “These companies are exploiting a loophole in US export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People’s Republic of China].
Nvidia says it works to prevent smuggling.
Megaspeed told the Journal that it conducts lawful business and designs its supply chain to comply with US export controls. Megaspeed added that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation.
Lutnick has come under fire since the revelations with critics on Capitol Hill questioning why the agency didn’t blacklist Megaspeed. Lutnick – whose job is speculated to be in jeopardy – is set to testify before the Senate about his agency’s handling of AI chip export controls.

articles.title_orig: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
articles.title_zh: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
articles.content_orig:
The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.
However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?
The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won’t launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA’s lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.
Given what is known publicly, and what Ars has heard privately, here are some educated guesses about all of this.
The first thing we can say for sure is that all estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt, including those in this article. Putting humans on any space vehicle is a difficult and time-consuming task, even outside of the requirements that NASA would impose for its astronauts.
The original target for launching humans on Starship (then known as the Interplanetary Transport System) set a decade ago was 2024. That was for a Mars mission. Then, in 2018 , SpaceX announced a lunar flyby mission on Starship with a target launch in 2023. This dearMoon mission was canceled in 2024. In 2022, SpaceX and Dennis Tito announced a lunar flyby mission later in the 2020s.
More recently, according to sources, SpaceX has been telling individuals interested in launching on Starship that it could begin offering flights by 2029. I probably would not put too much stock in this date.
All of this is to say, we cannot learn much from history other than to deeply discount any public launch dates on Starship for humans.
Most likely, the first humans to fly on Starship in space will do so after launching from Earth inside the NASA Orion spacecraft. Once in orbit they will then dock with Starship before transiting to the Moon, landing there in Starship, launching from the Moon back to Orion, and then returning to Earth inside NASA’s spacecraft.
NASA signed an agreement with SpaceX to develop Starship as this “Human Landing System” in 2021, with a lunar landing targeted for 2024. To no one’s surprise, this target has moved to 2028, and there remains considerable uncertainty about the viability of this date.
Nevertheless, the success of Saturday’s tower catch should help propel the Starship program toward a higher launch cadence, which is essential for lunar missions. It therefore seems plausible, but not certain, that humans could land on the Moon inside Starship before the end of this decade.
Again, how soon SpaceX achieves this target will depend upon its prioritization of a Human Landing System, among its other major goals to accomplish with Starship. At this point, SpaceX appears to be more focused on revenue-generating activities such as launching Starlink, and eventually, Starmind data center satellites.
Much has been made about the fact that Starship does not have a launch abort system—a feature of most human spacecraft that allows a crew vehicle to be rapidly pulled away from an exploding rocket.
This may not matter should SpaceX conduct its own human spaceflight missions. Unlike NASA, which imposes detailed human-rating requirements on vehicles carrying its astronauts, the Federal Aviation Administration does not certify commercial spacecraft as safe for passengers, instead operating under a regulatory framework that emphasizes informed consent and protection of the uninvolved public. Should SpaceX reach the point where it can launch Starship reliably, it will have the confidence it needs to press forward with human flights. Conceivably, this could happen within a few years.
According to potential customers, SpaceX is developing variants of the Human Landing System Starship for human flights, potentially carrying a few dozen people to the Moon. And such a prospect is tantalizing, for the interior of Starship’s pressurized cabin is almost unimaginably large for a spacecraft. A single Starship lunar lander has a pressurized habitable volume greater than the comparable volume of the International Space Station. This would be extraordinary.
Yet it is not a simple step to go from the current lunar lander design to an Earth lander. NASA’s lunar lander will never need to experience the tremendous heating of atmospheric reentry or perform the dramatic flip maneuver and propulsive landing that Starship uses to return home. Certifying those capabilities for human passengers, particularly on a vehicle without a traditional launch escape system, is an entirely different challenge.
Moreover, building a commercial human spaceflight business on Starship would be time-consuming and would likely not be nearly as profitable as launching Starlink satellites into space. And the risk is far greater—spaceflight remains dangerous, and the loss of a human crew would be a major negative for a publicly traded company. On the other hand, losing dozens of Starlink satellites on an errant launch would be a blip.
Despite Starship’s enormous theoretical capacity, SpaceX has also shown little interest in developing it as a crew transportation vehicle for commercial space stations in the near term. Several private space station operators have approached SpaceX about the possibility of Starship bringing astronauts to and from their stations. SpaceX indicated it was not interested.
Putting all of this together, I would not expect humans to land on Earth in Starship before 2030, and plausibly not until at least the mid-2030s.

articles.title_zh: Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centres (HDCs) in the USA—mainly driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence—has raised concerns about this industry’s carbon footprint. We compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centres operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources and attributable CO 2 emissions. Across facility-load scenarios, these HDCs consumed approximately 68–99 TWh of electricity and were associated with approximately 21–31 million metric tons of CO 2 under a location-based, total-output balancing-authority attribution method. Under the central scenario, HDC electricity demand was approximately 82 TWh, corresponding to about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption, and attributable CO 2 emissions were approximately 25.7 Mt. Roughly 54% of attributed generation was supplied by fossil-fuel sources. The HDC electricity-weighted total-output carbon intensity was approximately 314 gCO 2 kWh −1 , compared with a US total-output average of approximately 348 gCO 2 kWh −1 . Our approach provides a facility-resolved attributional framework for assessing the carbon footprint of hyperscale data centres using plant-level electricity-generation and emissions data.

Access to the restricted facility-level dataset may be considered for approved research collaborations, subject to the underlying data-use agreement, provider authorization and execution of an appropriate data-use agreement. Requests may be directed to the corresponding author. We provide public state- and balancing-authority-level data exports containing the electricity demand, attributable CO 2 emissions, total-output carbon intensity and attributed fuel mix used in the revised analysis. These aggregate exports reflect the central facility-load scenario ( u = 0.58) and the total-output attribution basis used for the headline results. They are available through the public reproducibility repository 46 . The repository exports, rather than the separate visualization interface, constitute the authoritative public data products for the revised analysis. Because the underlying facility data are protected by a data-use agreement, raw facility identifiers, addresses, coordinates and commercially sensitive facility attributes are not publicly released. The complete facility-level map-generation workflow requires authorized access to those inputs. Access to facility-level map coordinates remains subject to provider authorization and the data-use agreement; public aggregate files do not substitute for the restricted facility-level observations. Source data are provided with this paper.
All code used to estimate HDC power capacity, evaluate the capacity model, compute electricity use and emissions, validate public aggregate exports and reproduce manuscript-facing numerical results is publicly available in the public reproducibility repository 46 . A tagged snapshot corresponding to the Round 3 reproducibility materials is available as version v0.3.1-round3-final 47 . The repository contains: (1) the fully specified scikit-learn capacity-model pipeline, including disclosed predictors, preprocessing, effective hyperparameters, software version and evaluation metrics; (2) a non-identifying 403-row synthetic facility fixture with six missing power-capacity values; (3) a deterministic public synthetic split artefact at results/tables/synthetic_validation/splits.json , together with random and grouped validation outputs; (4) REPRO.md , documenting the validation sample, explicit imputation indicator, software versions, restricted-data workflow and emissions-accounting conventions; (5) scripts/reproduce_model.py , which regenerates the public synthetic validation outputs and writes the deterministic split artefact; (vi) the total-output emissions-attribution workflow using EPA eGRID2023 Revision 2; (7) denominator-audit, plant-inventory, public-export, restricted-data and manuscript-output validation scripts and (8) aggregate state- and balancing-authority-level exports used to verify the headline results. The public synthetic and aggregate materials allow external researchers to execute the capacity-model validation workflow, verify the emissions denominator, reproduce headline scenario totals, sum the public regional exports and run the repository tests without access to restricted facility records.

articles.title_zh: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase reports an issue that appears to be causing outages to online and in-person banking services
An issue with Chase banking services led to some customers of that institution and others reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds Monday.
The issues appeared to be affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The issues at Chase were caused by a “technical bug, not a cyber issue,” according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
A Zelle representative said that a technical issue on its platform originated with Chase.
“This is a Chase issue,” a Zelle spokesman told NBC News. “You need to speak to them.”
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
The outages were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade .
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.content_orig:
In the past week, shares of Nvidia ( NVDA -3.96% ) have been in a downward spiral. News that Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO and has been involved in multiple affairs, one of which may involve a Chinese spy, has significantly weighed on the company's valuation.
The stock has fallen so sharply that it is now trading at levels it hasn't been at since June of last year. Given how sudden and significant the sell-off has been, many investors are likely worried that there may still be worse to come. Could the tech stock fall to $100?
Image source: Getty Images.
When things are going well for a stock, the temptation is to assume it'll only continue to do well and rise higher. And when things are going poorly, many investors may fear that things will only get worse. Both outlooks, however, can be incredibly irrational. Sooner or later, the excitement or panic fades, and the stock stabilizes and may even end up going in the opposite direction.
Due to its sharp decline, Nvidia's stock is now trading at around 20 times its trailing earnings. And on a forward basis, based on analyst expectations of future earnings, its forward price-to-earnings multiple is just ten. That's an incredibly low valuation given that the S&P 500 average is a forward earnings multiple of 19.
The stock is already heavily discounted , and for a more significant decline to take place, one that takes it to $100, that would likely require there to be much more negative news around the tech business. And there would also likely need to be an all-out crash in the tech sector.
NASDAQ · As of 2:56 PM ET 11/16/26
The last time Nvidia's stock was at around $100 was after the Liberation Day tariffs were announced in April 2025. Global trade uncertainty weighed on not only Nvidia but the markets as a whole, and unless there's that kind of uncertainty and fear rattling the markets once more, I wouldn't expect Nvidia to fall to those levels anytime soon.
Nvidia is already an incredibly cheap-looking stock to buy given how well it has performed in recent years. Waiting for an even lower price could be risky for investors, because the risk is that it may never reach those levels; buying the stock now may be a much better move than holding out hope that it will fall even further.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.
